previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of multiple strokes, tracheostomy, GJ tube, atrial fibrillation, and diabetes was admitted after pulling out his GJ tube at the nursing home. He was monitored overnight and found to have mild leukocytosis without an identifiable source and reported leg pain. The GJ tube was successfully replaced by interventional radiology without complications. His atrial fibrillation was managed with continued warfarin, and his INR was monitored. A stage 2 sacral ulcer was noted but remained stable. He developed new edema in the right lower and upper extremities, prompting a recommendation for DVT ultrasound. He remained stable throughout the admission and was discharged to extended care with all medications continued as before.

FINDINGS:  Single supine AP portable view of the chest was obtained.  The
patient is rotated to the right.  Tracheostomy tube is again noted.  There is
blunting of the bilateral costophrenic angles, which could be due to trace
effusions.  Bibasilar atelectasis is seen.  Patchy left base opacity most
likely relates to atelectasis, although underlying aspiration or infection
cannot be excluded, however, has improved in the interval.  No overt pulmonary
edema is seen.  Cardiac and mediastinal silhouettes are stable.
